entries.title: Low-tide census at Cattle Point
entries.author: Maren Holt
entries.summary: A minus tide opened the lower shelf. Ochre stars in every crevice, and a single gumboot chiton the size of a shoe.
body: The tide bottomed out at 06:12, a little under minus two feet, and the lower shelf stayed dry for almost an hour. We worked the transect from the boulder field to the kelp line in twenty-metre sections.
Ochre stars were everywhere, mostly purple morphs, wedged into crevices on the north-facing side. We counted forty-one in the first section alone, which is well up on last August.
The find of the morning was a gumboot chiton near the kelp line, easily thirty centimetres long, rust-red and leathery. It did not move the whole time we watched it.

entries.title: First frost on the upper meadow
entries.author: Maren Holt
entries.summary: Rime on every lupine seed head before sunrise. The marmots had already gone quiet.
body: The thermometer at the trailhead read minus one when we arrived at dawn. The meadow was white with rime, every lupine seed head furred with it.
No marmot calls at all, which fits: the colony below the ridge has usually gone to ground by the third week of September.
By nine the frost had burned off everywhere except the shaded side of the talus slope.

entries.title: Chanterelle flush after the rain
entries.author: Theo Park
entries.summary: Three days of rain and the Douglas-fir duff is full of golden chanterelles. Also a patch of lobster mushrooms nobody expected.
body: After three days of steady rain the moss under the Douglas-firs was saturated, and the chanterelles came up in lines along the old root runs.
We logged sixty-two fruiting bodies in the plot, most of them young and firm. Near the creek crossing there was a patch of lobster mushrooms, bright orange against the moss.
Collected nothing; photographs and counts only.

entries.title: Heron rookery, late season
entries.author: Maren Holt
entries.summary: Most nests empty now, but two late broods are still being fed. Juveniles practising short flights between the alders.
body: Of the thirty-eight nests counted in May, only two still had young in them. Both broods looked close to fledging.
Several juveniles were making short, clumsy flights between the alders at the edge of the colony, landing badly and trying again.
The boardwalk closure sign can come down at the end of the month.

entries.title: Lichen survey on the old orchard fence
entries.author: Theo Park
entries.summary: Nine species on forty metres of split-rail fence, including a healthy colony of Methuselah's beard on the windward posts.
body: The split-rail fence along the old orchard is a lichen garden. We identified nine species on forty metres of rail.
The windward posts carry a long, pale colony of Methuselah's beard, which only grows where the air is clean.
Next visit: bring the hand lens with the better light.

entries.title: Coho moving up the creek
entries.author: Maren Holt
entries.summary: The first coho are holding in the pool below the footbridge. Eagles already lining the snags downstream.
body: Eleven coho were holding in the deep pool below the footbridge, waiting for the water to rise.
Five bald eagles on the snags downstream, which usually means the run is about to start in earnest.
Water temperature at the bridge: 11 °C.

entries.title: Moth sheet at the ranger cabin
entries.author: Theo Park
entries.summary: A white sheet and a lantern from ten until one. Twenty-three species, including a ceanothus silk moth that stayed until morning.
body: We hung the white sheet between two cedars and ran the lantern from ten until one.
Twenty-three species came in. The ceanothus silk moth arrived just before midnight and was still on the sheet at dawn.
Humidity was high and the wind never picked up, which may explain the numbers.

entries.title: Measuring the bull kelp canopy
entries.author: Maren Holt
entries.summary: Calm water let us paddle the full canopy edge. It has grown back past the reef for the first time in four summers.
body: A flat sea let us paddle the whole outer edge of the kelp bed with the GPS running.
The canopy now reaches past the outer reef, which it has not done since the marine heatwave four summers ago.
Sea urchin counts on the reef flat were the lowest we have recorded.
